ideas.title: RSS / Atom feed for the Changelog
ideas.problem: The Changelog is the only pull-back mechanism the site has — 'here's what changed' — but there is no machine-readable feed. Readers who want to follow updates must manually check the page. This breaks the return loop entirely for power users who live in feed readers.
ideas.proposal: Add a static `/rss.xml` route using Astro's built-in `@astrojs/rss` package (already in the Astro 4 ecosystem, zero new dependencies). At build time, iterate `CHANGELOG` entries (already a flat sorted array) and emit one `<item>` per entry. A matching `/zh/rss.xml` emits the same dates with `title[zh]` and `items[zh]` bullets. Add `<link rel='alternate' type='application/rss+xml'>` in `BaseLayout.astro` `<head>` and a small RSS icon link in `SiteFooter.astro` next to the tagline.
ideas.evidence: Changelog page already has all the data; feed readers are the canonical 'subscribe without email' flow for technical audiences who follow documentation wikis. MDN, the Rust blog, and Astro's own docs all ship RSS. The `/zh/` URL prefix pattern is already established for bilingual routes.
open_questions: Should each changelog item be a separate feed item, or one item per changelog entry (date + title + bullets)? One item per entry is simpler and matches how the changelog is structured.
Should the feed include content from all sections (new Field Guide chapters, Concepts, Deep-Dives) or only changelog entries? Changelog-only is the safe starting point.
Vercel caches static assets aggressively — does the feed need a `Cache-Control` header override in vercel.json to expire promptly after each deploy?
ideas.mockup_hint: Draw the footer of the page with the existing tagline text on the left and a small RSS icon (the standard orange square-wave icon) on the right linked to /rss.xml. In a separate inset, show the BaseLayout <head> with a <link rel='alternate' type='application/rss+xml' href='/rss.xml' title='Agentic AI Wiki Changelog'> tag. No modal, no banner — just the icon and the invisible head tag.

ideas.title: Copy-code button on code blocks
ideas.problem: The site has substantial code in `<pre class='standalone'>` blocks across Deep-Dives and Field Guide chapters. Readers must manually select and copy, which is friction on technical content. No browser renders a native copy affordance on pre-formatted blocks.
ideas.proposal: Inject a `<button class='copy-btn'>Copy</button>` into every `<pre>` block using a small `<script is:inline>` in `BaseLayout.astro` (or in the two detail layouts that host code: `ChapterLayout` and `SectionEntryLayout`). On click: read `pre.innerText`, write to `navigator.clipboard`, swap label to 'Copied' for 1.5 s, then reset. The button label is bilingual via a `data-copy` / `data-copied` attribute written by the same script using `document.documentElement.lang` to detect locale. Total JS: ~30 lines. The button is positioned absolutely top-right of the `<pre>` using existing CSS variables. No new dependency.
ideas.evidence: Widely expected on any technical documentation site; GitHub, MDN, and every major doc platform ships this. The Deep-Dives content has agent card JSON, Python snippets, and YAML configs — all prime candidates. The site already loads inline scripts (SiteSearch, tab-switcher) so the pattern is established. Content is rendered via `set:html` so the script must be DOM-traversal post-render rather than template-time.
open_questions: Should the button only appear on `<pre class='standalone'>` (the established code-block class) or on all `<pre>`? Scoping to `.standalone` avoids false positives on inline pre usage.
Clipboard API requires HTTPS (already the case on Vercel) and a secure context. Graceful degradation (hide button if API unavailable) is a one-liner.
Does stripping ANSI-style `<span class='c-*'>` syntax highlighting spans from innerText before copy cause any issues? `pre.innerText` naturally strips HTML tags — no extra processing needed.
ideas.mockup_hint: Draw a single `<pre>` code block (dark background, monospace text showing a JSON agent card snippet). In the top-right corner of the block, show a small pill-shaped button labeled 'Copy' with a clipboard icon. In a 'before/after' panel next to it, show the button changed to a checkmark and 'Copied!' after clicking. The button should appear only on hover (CSS opacity transition). Show both EN ('Copy' / 'Copied!') and ZH ('复制' / '已复制') label variants in a note.

ideas.title: End-of-article CTA: 'Graduate to' block
ideas.problem: Every concept and deep-dive article ends with prev/next within-section navigation — good for sequential readers but insufficient for the reader who just finished 'What is RAG?' and wants to know what to read next in a different section. The cross-section relationship (Concept → Deep-Dive → Field Guide chapter) is unmapped at the page level. Readers reach the end of an article and have no obvious escalation path.
ideas.proposal: Add an optional `graduate` field (array of `{ section: 'field-guide'|'concepts'|'deep-dives', slug: string }`) to the manifest `Entry` type for Concepts and Deep-Dives. At the bottom of `SectionEntryLayout`, if `entry.graduate` is non-empty, render a small card row titled 'Go deeper →' (EN) / '深入了解 →' (ZH) that links to those entries. Fall back gracefully: if `graduate` is absent, the card simply does not render. No backend, no analytics — purely manifest-driven. The `graduate` links resolve at build time using existing `ENTRIES` + `CHAPTERS` lookups, so dead links are build errors.
ideas.evidence: The NAVIGATION-PLAN.md explicitly calls this out as P2 ('Related pages') and P3 ('prev/next + graduate to'). This proposal is a scoped, lower-effort version of P2 that uses a separate `graduate` field rather than the heavier `related: slug[]` mechanism, making it easier to add incrementally. High-value pairs already identified in NAVIGATION-PLAN: RAG → Advanced RAG Architectures; Agent Loop → ReAct; Tool Calling → Tool-Calling Standards; Agentic Risks → Agentic Threat Model.
open_questions: Should `graduate` be added to the manifest `Entry` type (schema change, touches verify script) or delivered as a separate static map file? A separate map avoids touching the manifest schema but is less elegant.

Field Guide chapters use a different manifest shape (CHAPTERS/PARTS). Should `graduate` be one-directional (Concepts → Deep-Dives, Concepts → Field Guide) or bidirectional? Starting one-directional is simpler.
How many graduate links are too many? Suggest capping at 3 to keep the card compact.
ideas.mockup_hint: Draw the bottom of a concept detail page (e.g. 'What is RAG?') below the article text and above the prev/next nav. Show a lightly bordered card row titled 'Go deeper →' with two entry cards side by side: one for a Deep-Dive ('Advanced RAG Architectures') and one for a Field Guide chapter ('Retrieval'). Each card has a small section kicker label ('Deep-Dive' / 'Field Guide') in the accent color above the entry title. The ZH locale shows '深入了解 →' as the heading and Chinese entry titles.

ideas.title: Persistent reading progress via localStorage
ideas.problem: The Field Guide is a 22-chapter linear course. There is no indication of how far a reader has progressed, and returning readers must remember or scroll the sidebar to find where they left off. The home page always shows 'Start reading →' with no personalisation — it cannot distinguish a first-time visitor from someone 18 chapters in.
ideas.proposal: On each Field Guide chapter page, write `localStorage.setItem('fg-last', slug)` on DOMContentLoaded (inline script, no library). On the home page and the field-guide index, read `localStorage.getItem('fg-last')` and if set, replace 'Start reading →' with 'Continue: <chapter title> →' linking to that chapter. In `ChapterSidebar`, mark already-visited slugs (stored as a JSON array in `localStorage.setItem('fg-visited', [...])`) with a subtle checkmark or filled dot. All logic is ~25 lines of vanilla JS in existing `<script is:inline>` slots. Bilingual: chapter titles come from the already-rendered page data attributes (`data-title-en`, `data-title-zh`) or from reading `document.documentElement.lang`.
ideas.evidence: Linear courses (Learn X in Y Minutes, MDN Learn, freeCodeCamp) universally track progress because it is the single biggest drop-off point: people forget where they left off and give up. The Field Guide is structured exactly like a course — 6 parts, 22 ordered chapters — making it the ideal candidate. No backend, no auth: localStorage is exactly the right primitive.
open_questions: Should the 'Continue reading' link replace or supplement 'Start reading →' on the home page? Supplementing (showing both) is safer and clearer.
How should visited state be represented in the sidebar — a dot, a checkmark, a strikethrough? A small filled dot matching the existing sidebar dot style is the least invasive option.
Should progress reset on the ZH locale independently from EN, or share state? Separate keys (`fg-last-en` / `fg-last-zh`) make locale switching clean.
ideas.mockup_hint: Draw two states of the home page featured card side by side. Left: first-time visitor — card shows 'Start reading →'. Right: returning visitor who left off at chapter 12 — card shows 'Continue: Observability & Tracing →' with a small progress indicator '12 / 22 chapters'. Below that, draw the ChapterSidebar with the first 11 chapters showing a small filled circle (visited) and chapter 12 highlighted as current. Chapters 13-22 have empty circles.

ideas.title: Search keyboard shortcut discoverability
ideas.problem: Pagefind search is wired and functional but the trigger is a small button in the top-right header with no visual keyboard hint. Power users who know `/` or Cmd/Ctrl-K exists get instant access, but the keyboard shortcut is entirely undiscoverable. On every content page, search is the fastest path to adjacent material, but most readers will not find it by experiment.
ideas.proposal: Add a keyboard hint badge to the search trigger button: render `<kbd>/</kbd>` or `<kbd>⌘K</kbd>` next to the 'Search' label in `SiteSearch.astro`. The badge is CSS-only (border + monospace), hidden on small screens (< 640 px) via a media query, and no JS is needed. Additionally, add a visually-styled 'Search the wiki' input-lookalike (non-interactive, click opens the modal) as a prominent bar on the `/field-guide` and `/concepts` index pages — not on every page, to avoid clutter. Bilingual: the badge text is language-agnostic (`/` and `⌘K` are universal symbols); the placeholder text uses the existing `t.search.placeholder` string.
ideas.evidence: GitHub, Linear, Notion, and every major developer tool shows the keyboard shortcut inline on the search trigger. The shortcut code already exists in SiteSearch.astro (lines 139–149). The Pagefind index is built and working; the barrier is discoverability, not capability. NAVIGATION-PLAN explicitly says 'Search prominence — Pagefind is wired; is it discoverable from every page or only the index?' as an open question.
open_questions: Should the kbd hint show '/' or '⌘K'? Show both: '/' on its own on desktop, then '⌘K' as an alternative. macOS vs Windows: ⌘ vs Ctrl — the existing JS already handles both, but the badge could show just '/' which works universally.

Should the fake search bar on index pages be a full-width bar or a compact element? A compact 320px bar centered below the page intro, consistent with the existing `.wrap` max-width system, is tasteful.
Does adding a prominent search bar on the Field Guide index duplicate the header trigger confusingly? Label it 'Search chapters and concepts…' to distinguish scope.
ideas.mockup_hint: Draw the site header with the search button. On the right of the 'Search' label, show a small <kbd>/</kbd> badge with a light border and monospace font. On a separate panel below, draw the Field Guide index page with a centered fake-input bar ('Search the wiki… /') between the page intro and the chapter list — like the GitHub search bar. Both elements are shown in EN and ZH variants side by side, with the ZH version showing '搜索本维基… /'.

Readers who want to share a specific insight with a colleague must share the top-level URL and say 'scroll to section 3'. There are no anchor links on headings and no share affordances below article level.

ideas.evidence: MDN, CSS-Tricks, and Smashing Magazine all do heading anchors. The wiki already has well-structured HTML with `<h2 class='phase'>` / `<h3 class='step'>` headings in content fragments. Deep-Dive essays are particularly long (5-7 steps each) and benefit most. This costs zero backend resources and works purely client-side.

ideas.title: Richer site footer with section navigation and 'New this week'
ideas.problem: The current footer is a single line: tagline + copyright. It is a dead end — readers who reach the bottom of any page (home, about, changelog, index pages) have nowhere to go except back up. The footer is also identical on every page, offering no contextual next steps. There is no at-a-glance indicator of recent activity on the site.
ideas.proposal: Expand `SiteFooter.astro` into a three-column grid (collapses to stacked on mobile): (1) brand column with tagline and RSS icon link; (2) 'Explore' nav column with links to all four sections (Field Guide, Concepts, Deep-Dives, Changelog) — all locale-aware via `localizeHref`; (3) 'Recently added' column showing the 2 most recent changelog entry titles (already fetched in `HomeView` — the same import can be passed as a prop or re-imported in the footer). All data is static / build-time. Bilingual: column headings added to `ui.ts` as `footer.explore` and `footer.recent`; entry titles already carry `[locale]`. The footer uses existing CSS variables (no new stylesheet rules beyond the three-column layout).
ideas.evidence: Every mature documentation site (MDN, Stripe docs, Vercel docs) has a footer with section navigation. The current footer wastes a high-visibility zone that every reader reaches at the end of a session — it is the last impression. The 'Recently added' column gives return visitors an instant signal that there is new content, increasing the probability they click to the changelog and come back next week.
open_questions: Should the footer import `CHANGELOG` directly (adds a static data import to every page's bundle via the layout) or should the top-level pages pass recent entries down as a prop? Direct import is simpler and negligible in bundle size since it is build-time data.
Three columns may be too wide for a site with a constrained max-width. Should it be two columns (brand+nav | recent) or three? Two is safer on narrow viewports.
Should the RSS link appear in the footer only after the RSS feed (engagement-01) is implemented, or is a placeholder acceptable? Placeholder with a comment is fine — they ship as one PR.
ideas.mockup_hint: Draw the full-width site footer as a three-column layout on a light background. Left column: 'Agentic AI Wiki' brand name in Fraunces serif, the tagline below it, and a small RSS icon link. Middle column: heading 'Explore' (bold small-caps) above a list of four nav links — Field Guide, Concepts, Deep-Dives, Changelog — each in the accent color. Right column: heading 'Recently added' with two changelog entry titles and their dates below (e.g., '2026-05-19 — Cross-page links between related topics'). A thin top border separates the footer from the page body. Below the three columns, a centered copyright line. Show the ZH locale variant with '探索', '最新更新' headings.

notes:
Key findings from the audit:

1. ENGAGEMENT DESERT: Every page ends the same way — prev/next buttons then a one-line footer. The only re-engagement hook is the Changelog section on the home page (2 latest entries). There are zero subscription, share, or progress mechanics anywhere.

2. FOOTER IS WASTED SPACE: `SiteFooter.astro` is 11 lines, one div, one string. It is the lowest-effort, highest-visibility fix on the list (engagement-07).

3. RSS IS THE OBVIOUS MISSING PRIMITIVE: The Changelog exists and is structured data. @astrojs/rss is in the Astro ecosystem. This is a 1-2 hour implementation that unlocks the entire class of 'subscribe to updates' behavior without email, without a CMP, without a backend (engagement-01).

4. SEARCH EXISTS BUT IS HIDDEN: Pagefind is fully wired with keyboard shortcuts (/, Cmd/Ctrl-K) but there is zero visual hint. The shortcut code is at SiteSearch.astro lines 139-149 and never surfaces to readers (engagement-05).

5. FIELD GUIDE IS A COURSE WITHOUT PROGRESS TRACKING: 22 chapters, linear order, and zero persistence. localStorage is the exact right primitive here (engagement-04).

6. CONSIDERED AND DROPPED:
   - Newsletter signup (Buttondown): Dropped. The site has no existing email capture flow and the maintainer contact is GitHub/LinkedIn. A Buttondown embed would require an iframe or JS from an external domain, which is a meaningful security/trust step given the site's 'content is code' philosophy. Better introduced after RSS demonstrates subscriber demand.
   - 'Cite this page' BibTeX block: Interesting but low urgency — the audience is practitioners, not academics. Deferred to a later research pass.
   - In-page feedback thumbs: Without a backend, the only options are localStorage (local-only, no aggregate signal) or counter.dev (external JS). Neither is compelling enough vs. the other ideas. Dropped.
   - 'New since you last visited' banner: Compelling concept but requires comparing localStorage timestamp against feed dates, which depends on RSS (engagement-01) shipping first. Noted as a follow-on to engagement-01.
   - 'Save for later' bookmarks: Nice to have, but the site already has a clear reading order (Field Guide) and the use case overlaps heavily with browser bookmarks. Low incremental value vs. engagement-04 (progress tracking).

7. OVERLAP WITH NAVIGATION-PLAN: engagement-03 ('Graduate to' block) is a scoped version of NAVIGATION-PLAN P2 (Related pages). The research explicitly notes this and positions it as the engagement-lens framing of a known structural gap, so the two teams can coordinate on manifest schema changes.
